title: The third rooms
hook: the well-ordered life that can still be a little too careful

segments.voice: Yesterday, falling: you slip, and you don't turn back. Today, the rooms of people who are doing everything right.

Here's a certain kind of person. Up on time. Bills paid. Goes to Mass, gives to the collection, volunteers twice a year, never raises their voice. A good person, genuinely, with a life organized like a well-kept kitchen drawer. And yet sometimes, when something is asked that doesn't fit the drawer, a big risk, a messy person, a sudden need, they get very quiet and very reasonable. Teresa of Ávila built a whole set of rooms in her castle for these good, careful people. She's fond of them. And she's worried about them.
screen: `A GOOD, CAREFUL LIFE.` → `A WELL-KEPT DRAWER.` → `WHEN SOMETHING DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: First, the praise. The people in the third rooms, Teresa says, have come a long way. They avoid sin, even small ones. They spend time in prayer. They're kind, they give, they keep their homes and lives in order. She calls this a real blessing, and she means it. Second, the young man. A rich young man comes to Jesus. He's kept every commandment since he was a boy. Jesus invites him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. And, in the Douay-Rheims: "when the young man had heard this word, he went away sad: for he had great possessions." Teresa says he stays on her mind the whole time she writes about these rooms. Good all the way through, and then, at the one moment that asks for everything, a little too careful to let go. Third, the reason. Their love, she says, isn't yet strong enough to overwhelm their reason. Everything is sensible. Even their penances are as orderly as their lives. They worry about their health, their reputation, what could go wrong. And when a trial comes, they're surprised and hurt, because they've been so good. Fourth, the way on. Teresa's advice is humility, and a little daring. Stop measuring how far you've come. Don't wait until you can see the whole path before taking a step. Her worry, in a picture: a clean house is a good thing, but love sometimes means opening the door when someone knocks at a bad time. Tidy is good. Tidy is not the same as holy.
screen: `GOOD, ORDERLY, GENEROUS LIVES.` · `THE RICH YOUNG MAN WALKS AWAY.` · `REASON STILL STRONGER THAN LOVE.` · `A LITTLE DARING.` · then, large: `HE WENT AWAY SAD.`

segments.voice: Ask where your life is a little too careful: a gift you keep meaning to give, a person you avoid because they're messy, a yes you keep postponing until things are calmer. Let one come to mind, and choose one generous thing you could do about it, slightly more than feels sensible. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, just decide.
Possessions. What the rich young man couldn't let go of when Jesus asked for everything, and what still holds back careful, orderly lives today. Today's word.
Your line: tidy isn't holy. A good life is a start, not a stopping place. That's two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic retreat leaders often use Teresa's third dwelling places to help faithful, church-going people ask where their good habits have become too cautious, and what generous risk love might ask of them.

chat.says: I'm a good, organized person. What's Teresa's worry about people like me?
options: That being careful can make you hold back when love asks for something risky.
That organized people are secretly bad and their good habits count for nothing.
That they spend too long in prayer and should do more practical work instead.
chat.meaning: Teresa praises the third rooms' goodness, but like the rich young man, careful people can hold back. Tidy is good; it isn't the same as holy.

notes: Check Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 19:22 ('And when the young man had heard this word, he went away sad: for he had great possessions.').

Teresa's description of the third dwelling places (avoiding sin, ordered lives, 'love not yet strong enough to overwhelm reason', penances as ordered as their lives, being upset by trials) paraphrased from III.1–2; confirm.
The rich young man is Teresa's own example in III.1; confirm.
'Tidy isn't holy' is the index carry; the script frames it as a paraphrase of Teresa's concern, not her words.
